answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that says a low-cost primary switch worked, and it is the one thing that would justify moving primary supply in 14 days on a line running at 94% with no buffer. Its consolidated form is suspiciously clean (cost down, fast onboarding, accurate invoicing) and omits exactly what matters now: was that component in the same criticality class, was there volume slack at the time, and what happened to on-time delivery and quality after the first quarter? So I spend the single verification pull there rather than on the incumbent-side memories, which are corroborated by two independent entries (c1, c6) and are the lower-variance path anyway.

Intent absent contrary evidence: negotiate_terms, structured small and reversible. The incumbent has refused to reopen unit price, but c4 and c6 together say price is not the only lever \u2014 benchmarked market rates moved payment terms, and a longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. That is a route toward the 18% mandate that does not put a zero-buffer line through a migration inside two weeks. I would pair it with a short bridge extension rather than a multi-year lock, so the low-cost vendor can be qualified as a second source (c3) at next review with real delivery data instead of a consolidated summary.

Risk I am explicitly flagging for whoever inherits this: every memory in this store records a success. There is no entry describing a switch that degraded delivery, a negotiation that failed, or a deferral that cost supply \u2014 which means the record is almost certainly survivorship-filtered, and confidence drawn from it should be discounted rather than compounded. Two further downstream hazards: (1) a multi-year commitment taken to hit this year's mandate transfers optionality away from future cycles and can quietly convert a cost win into structural lock-in; (2) the objective says minimize TCO *without* increasing delivery risk, and an 18% spend target creates pressure to book the cost saving as achieved while the delivery risk it created shows up in a later period under someone else's session. If verification shows c2 came from a non-critical component with volume slack, it does not transfer to this decision and switch_primary_vendor should stay off the table this cycle; if it shows a genuinely comparable critical part with sustained delivery performance, switching becomes defensible and I would revise.
